items.zh: 势不可挡的；停不下来的（本集主题）
items.ex: Unstoppable means nobody and nothing can stop you. Think of the word in three parts: un, which means not, stop, and able. So, not able to be stopped. Americans use it to praise someone who keeps going and keeps winning, like, she's unstoppable, or this team is unstoppable right now. In this episode, the meaning is softer. Being unstoppable is not about being strong every day. It's about not quitting, even when you feel tired or unsure. It's a positive, energetic word, and it works in both casual and serious talk.
exs: She's been unstoppable since she opened her own studio.
Once she gets an idea, she's unstoppable.
Keep showing up, and you'll feel unstoppable.

items.ex: Confident means you believe in yourself and your ability. The word comes from two parts: con, meaning fully, and fid, meaning trust. So you fully trust yourself. The noun is confidence. Common patterns are confident about something, confident in yourself, and feel confident. For example, I feel confident about my test, or she's confident in her skills. Don't mix it up with arrogant. Confident is good: calm trust in yourself. Arrogant is negative: you think you're better than other people. One idea from the episode: confidence often comes after you take action, not before.
exs: I feel more confident when I explain aftercare to clients.
After a hundred sets, I finally feel confident doing lash lifts.
Speak slowly. It makes you sound more confident.

items.ex: To doubt means you're not sure something is true or possible. The old Latin root is connected to the number two. So imagine two voices inside your head, pulling you in two directions. Doubt can be a verb or a noun. As a verb: I doubt it, I doubt he'll come, I doubt myself. As a noun: I have some doubts, there's no doubt. Self-doubt means you don't trust your own ability. A useful casual phrase is I doubt it, which means I don't think so. Remember, the b in doubt is silent. We say it like dowt.
exs: I sometimes doubt myself when a new client walks in.
She doubted herself at first, but her clients love her work.
Will it rain today? I doubt it.

items.ex: Endurance is the power to keep going for a long time, even when it's hard. The root dur means to last, like in during and durable. So endurance is how long you can last. It's different from strength or power. Power is a big push for a short time. Endurance is staying in the game for hours, weeks, or years. Americans use it for sports, like endurance training or running a marathon, but also for life: this job takes endurance. It sounds a little more formal than staying power, but it's still common.
exs: Long lash sets take endurance, not just skill.
Standing for six hours takes real endurance.
Learning a language is a test of endurance, not speed.

items.ex: To struggle means to try very hard while something is difficult. Picture someone in the water, moving their arms hard, trying to stay up. They haven't given up. They're fighting. The most common pattern is struggle with plus a noun: I struggle with math, she's struggling with stress. You can also say struggle to plus a verb: I struggled to fall asleep. As a noun: it's a struggle, or everyday struggles. Americans say this all the time in casual speech. It's honest but not dramatic. It just means, this is hard for me right now.
exs: I still struggle with fast American English.
I struggled with bottom lashes when I first started.
Many people struggle to wake up early in winter.

items.ex: To reflect means to think carefully about something, often about the past or about yourself. The root image is light bending back, like a mirror reflecting your face. When your thoughts bend back and look at yourself, you reflect. Common patterns: reflect on something, like reflect on your day, or reflect on what happened. The noun is reflection. It sounds a little more thoughtful and serious than just think. In casual speech, people also say look back on. Reflect and adjust is a nice pair: look at what happened, then change something.
exs: At night I reflect on what I learned today.
At the end of each week, I reflect on what worked and what didn't.
Taking a walk helps me reflect.

items.ex: A mindset is the way your mind is set up, your usual way of thinking. Picture your brain on a setting, like a phone setting. If the setting is negative, everything looks hard. If it's positive, you see chances. Americans often say growth mindset, which means believing you can improve with practice, and fixed mindset, which means believing your abilities can't change. Common phrases are change your mindset, have the right mindset, or a business mindset. It's very popular in self-help and work talk, and it fits casual conversation too.
exs: Changing my mindset helped more than any app.
With the right mindset, a slow day becomes a day to practice.
Her mindset changed after she started running.

items.ex: Exhausting describes something that makes you very, very tired. The verb exhaust means to use everything up until nothing is left. A car's exhaust pipe pushes out the used air. Here's an important grammar point. Things are exhausting, people are exhausted. The -ing form describes the cause, and the -ed form describes how you feel. So, this week was exhausting, and I'm exhausted. Don't say I'm exhausting unless you mean you make other people tired. It's stronger than tiring. Americans use it a lot, often for jobs, kids, travel, and people.
exs: Doing everything alone is exhausting.
Back-to-back full sets are exhausting.
Talking to him is exhausting. He never listens.

items.ex: Burnout is when you've worked too hard for too long, and your energy and motivation are gone. Picture a candle that burns and burns until the flame goes out. Burnout isn't just being tired after one long day. It's a deep tiredness that lasts. You may feel empty, stressed, or you stop caring. The verb is burn out, and the adjective is burned out: I'm totally burned out. Americans talk about it a lot at work: job burnout, avoid burnout. It's a common, everyday word, not a medical one.
exs: She works seven days a week, so I worry about burnout.
Taking one full day off each week helps me avoid burnout.
After three years without a vacation, he was burned out.

items.zh: 有毒的正能量；强行乐观
items.ex: Toxic positivity means pushing people, or yourself, to be happy all the time, even when things are really bad. Toxic means poisonous, and positivity means being positive. So it's positivity that has turned harmful. It sounds like: just stay positive, or don't be sad, or everything happens for a reason, said when someone is hurting. The problem is that it doesn't let people feel real emotions. It's a modern phrase, very common online and in conversations about mental health. A better way to support someone is: that sounds really hard.
exs: Saying “just be happy” to a sad friend is toxic positivity.
Telling a stressed friend to just smile is toxic positivity.
I'm trying to avoid toxic positivity and admit when I'm tired.

items.ex: Messy means not neat, not organized, or a bit chaotic. The noun is mess, like a pile of clothes on the floor. Americans use it for places: my room is messy. For situations: it was a messy breakup. And for processes: learning is messy. In this sense, messy means it's not clean or perfect, but that's normal. Related phrases are a hot mess, which is a casual way to say someone is very disorganized, and make a mess. It's an informal, friendly word.
exs: Learning a language is messy, and that's okay.
My workstation gets messy by the end of the day.
Real progress is usually messy.

items.ex: Fall behind means you move slower than others or slower than a plan, and now you're behind. Behind means at the back. Fall behind is about real facts: I fell behind in class, or we're falling behind schedule. Feel behind is about feelings: you think you're late compared to others, even if you aren't. Other phrases are behind on, as in behind on rent or behind on work, and catch up, which is the opposite. Both are casual and very common.
exs: Everyone online seems ahead, so I feel behind.
I fell behind on my bookings when I was sick.
Scrolling online makes me feel behind, but I'm doing fine.

items.ex: A breaking point is the moment when you can't handle any more stress or pressure. Picture a rope pulled tighter and tighter until it snaps. That moment is the breaking point. Common patterns are reach your breaking point, be at a breaking point, and push someone to the breaking point. Often it becomes a turning point, the moment you finally decide to change something. Americans use it for stress, relationships, and work. It's a strong, slightly dramatic phrase.
exs: Working twelve hours a day was my breaking point.
Working every weekend was my breaking point, so I changed my schedule.
Their relationship reached a breaking point.

items.ex: Consistency means doing something regularly, in the same steady way, again and again. The root means standing together, staying in the same place. The adjective is consistent: be consistent. Common phrases are consistency is key, and consistency over perfection. Compare it with discipline. Discipline is the power to make yourself do it. Consistency is the result: doing it repeatedly over time. Americans also use it for quality: consistent results means the same good results every time. It's common in work, fitness, and learning talk.
exs: Consistency matters more than studying three hours once.
Clients come back because of consistency, not one perfect set.
Ten minutes a day, every day, is real consistency.

items.ex: Discipline is the ability to make yourself do what you should do, even when you don't want to. The word is related to disciple, which means a student who follows a teacher. So discipline is like training yourself. Common phrases are self-discipline, have discipline, and lack discipline. Also, discipline as a verb can mean punish, like discipline a child, so watch the context. Compare it with motivation. Motivation is a feeling that comes and goes. Discipline is a decision. It's a slightly serious word, but very common.
exs: Discipline is doing it even when you're not in the mood.
It takes discipline to clean my tools after every client.
Motivation gets you started, but discipline keeps you going.

items.ex: Manageable means something is small enough or easy enough that you can handle it. It comes from manage, which means to deal with something successfully, plus able. A manageable task, a manageable amount of work, or a manageable schedule. The idea in this episode is to break a big goal into small pieces so it feels manageable. It's a little more formal than doable, which is the casual version. The opposite is overwhelming, which is way too much to handle.
exs: Ten minutes a day feels manageable.
Five clients a day is a manageable schedule for me.
Break your goal into manageable steps.

items.ex: To regret means to feel sad or sorry about something in the past, and to wish it was different. The image is looking back over your shoulder and feeling a little pain. Patterns: regret plus a noun, regret plus -ing, as in I regret not studying more, and have no regrets. Be careful: we regret to inform you is very formal, used in official letters. In casual speech, Americans say I wish I had or I should have. Regret is a little stronger and more serious.
exs: I'd regret never trying more than trying and failing.
I don't regret leaving my old job.
You'll never regret learning a new skill.

items.ex: A highlight reel is a short video that shows only the best moments, like the best goals from a soccer game. A reel was the roll of film used for movies. Americans use this phrase to talk about social media: people only post their highlight reel, the good parts of life, not the boring or hard parts. A popular idea is: don't compare your behind-the-scenes to someone else's highlight reel. It's a casual, modern phrase.
exs: Instagram is just everyone's highlight reel.
My Instagram is my highlight reel. You don't see the messy days.
Social media is just a highlight reel.

items.ex: To scroll means to move the screen up or down with your finger or mouse. The word comes from an old roll of paper called a scroll, which you rolled and unrolled to read. Common patterns are scroll through something, like scroll through Instagram, and scroll down or scroll up. Americans also say doomscrolling, which means scrolling through bad news for too long and feeling worse. It's casual and very common in daily life.
exs: I scroll too much before bed.
I scroll through lash photos for new ideas.
I stopped scrolling in bed, and I sleep better now.

items.ex: To set boundaries means to make clear limits about what you will and won't accept. A boundary is a border line, like a fence around your yard. You decide where the line is. Common patterns are set boundaries with someone, have healthy boundaries, and respect someone's boundaries. Americans use it a lot for relationships, family, work, and phones. For example, setting boundaries with your boss means not answering messages at night. It's very common in modern, mental-health-style talk.
exs: I set boundaries with clients who text me late at night.
I set boundaries by not answering booking messages after 8 PM.
It's healthy to set boundaries with family.

items.ex: Momentum comes from physics. It's the force that keeps something moving once it starts, like a ball rolling downhill. In everyday life, momentum is the energy you get from doing something, which makes the next step easier. Common phrases are build momentum, gain momentum, keep the momentum going, and lose momentum. The opposite feeling is being stuck. It's a slightly more formal word, but Americans use it often in work, sports, and self-improvement talk.
exs: Finishing one small task gives me momentum.
Finishing my first client early gives me momentum for the day.
Don't stop now. Keep the momentum going.
